title: The school under trees
hook: Tagore founded a school at Santiniketan where classes met outdoors
tomorrow: what did Tagore want his very last words to be?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: moments, and enough. The butterfly counts moments, not months, and has time enough. Today, a strange choice by a man who couldn't stand classrooms, and a puzzle hidden in where he put the desks. Or didn't.

Plenty of people who hated school swear they'll never set foot in one again. Tagore did the opposite. In his memoir he remembers the schools of his boyhood as dreary places he slipped away from, one after another, and he never finished. Then, as a grown man, he started a school of his own, at Santiniketan, on the land of his father's ashram. And here's the odd detail: the classes met outdoors, under the trees.
screen: `NEVER SETTING FOOT IN ONE AGAIN.` → `ONE SCHOOL AFTER ANOTHER.` → `HE STARTED HIS OWN.` → `CLASSES UNDER THE TREES.`

segments.voice: Why would a school-hater build a school? Because what he hated wasn't learning. In an essay called My School, he describes the schools he knew as something like factories, shutting children away from the very world they were meant to be learning about. So he reached back to a picture much older than any classroom: the tapovana, the forest hermitage of ancient India, where students lived near their teacher among trees, under open sky. In another essay, The Religion of the Forest, Tagore argues that India's early wisdom grew up in forests rather than cities, and that it sought harmony with all of life instead of conquest of it. That's the teaching, as Tagore read the world of the Upanishads: knowledge isn't something stored behind walls. It's a kind of sympathy with everything, and nature is a teacher, not a backdrop. Last week's same stream, turned into a school day. So the children at Santiniketan sat on the ground beneath the trees, and their days moved with the weather and the seasons. It sounds charming, and it was: lessons with birdsong, a teacher's voice carrying over the grass. It was also an argument. If the same life runs through you and the tree, then learning beside the tree isn't a field trip. It's the whole point.
screen: `SCHOOLS LIKE FACTORIES.` · `THE TAPOVANA: A FOREST HERMITAGE.` · `HARMONY, NOT CONQUEST.` · `NATURE AS TEACHER.` · then, large: `UNDER THE TREES.`

segments.voice: If you can, step outside or go to a window, and choose one tree or plant. For two minutes, look at it as if it were today's teacher: the shape of one leaf, where the light lands, what moves. Let it teach you one thing, without rushing to name it.
The school under trees: Tagore's school at Santiniketan, where classes met outdoors, modeled on the forest hermitages of ancient India, with nature as one of the teachers.
Your line: under the trees. Tagore's classroom had no walls, and that was entirely on purpose. Talk soon.
